q: 1. The relation between modulus of rupture fcr and characteristic strength of concrete fck is given by ...........
explain: As per IS:456, the flexural strength of concrete is calculated using the formula 0.7 * sqrt(fck).

q: 2. The most commonly use admixture which prolongs the setting and hardening time is ...........
explain: Gypsum is added during cement manufacturing to act as a retarder, preventing the 'flash set' of C3A.

q: 3. The increase in strength of concrete after six months is generally ...........
explain: Over a six-month period, the continuous hydration of cement typically adds about 20% to the 28-day strength.

q: 4. The decrease in stress caused in a pre-stressed beam at constant strain is called ...........
explain: Relaxation is the time-dependent decrease of stress in steel held at a constant strain.

q: 5. The advantage of concrete is that ...........
options: it can be moulded into any shape and size
it is durable and maintenance cost is practically nil
explain: Concrete is versatile, durable, and naturally fire-resistant, offering all these structural benefits.

q: 6. The modulus of elasticity of steel is generally taken as ...........
explain: The standard value for the modulus of elasticity of all types of reinforcing steel is 200 kN/mm² or 200,000 N/mm².

q: 7. The design load obtained after multiplying the characteristic load by the partial safety factor is also known as ...........
explain: In Limit State Design, the design load is the factored load (Characteristic Load x γf).

q: 8. In the limit state method, the maximum strain in concrete in bending compression is taken to be ...........
explain: IS:456 specifies that the maximum compressive strain in the outermost fiber of concrete in bending is 0.0035.

q: 9. In the case of Fe 415 and Fe 500 steels, the yield stress is taken as ....... percent proof stress.
explain: High-strength steels do not have a well-defined yield point, so the yield stress is taken as the stress corresponding to a 0.2% permanent (offset) strain.

q: 10. Over reinforced section is not desirable because ...........
options: failure is sudden as concrete fails first
explain: In over-reinforced sections, concrete reaches its failure strain before the steel yields, leading to a brittle, explosive failure without warning.

q: 11. Which of the following is not a measure adopted for reducing deflection?
explain: Decreasing reinforcement would actually increase deflection; to reduce it, one should increase stiffness (depth or concrete grade) or use camber.

q: 12. The stresses caused by different loads can be superimposed in ...........
explain: Superposition is only valid in linear-elastic systems. Working Stress Method is the only one listed that assumes linear elasticity.

q: 13. The approximate allowable stress in axial compression in reinforced concrete is ...........
explain: In WSM, the permissible stress in direct (axial) compression (sigma_cc) is roughly $f_{ck}/4$, which is $0.25 \cdot f_{ck}$.

q: 14. If the modular ratio is m, steel ratio is r = sigma_st / nbc and overall depth of a beam is d, the depth of the critical neutral axis of the beam is ...........
explain: Derived from the properties of similar triangles in the stress diagram of a balanced section: $x_c = [m \cdot \sigma_{cbc} / (m \cdot \sigma_{cbc} + \sigma_{st})] \cdot d$.

q: 15. In a singly reinforced beam, the effective depth is measured from the compression edge to the ............
explain: Effective depth ($d$) is the distance from the extreme compression fiber to the centroid (center) of the tensile reinforcement.

q: 16. A reinforced concrete beam will crack if tensile stress set up in the concrete below the neutral axis is ............
explain: Cracking occurs as soon as the actual tensile stress in the concrete fibers exceeds its allowable tensile capacity (modulus of rupture).

q: 17. In an over-reinforced section ............
options: steel reinforcement is not fully stressed
explain: In an over-reinforced section, concrete reaches its maximum permissible stress before the steel, meaning the steel remains under-stressed.

q: 18. For an over reinforced (singly reinforced) rectangular reinforced concrete section ............
options: lever arm is less than balanced section
max steel stress = allowable steel stress
max concrete stress = allowable concrete stress
explain: By definition, an over-reinforced section fails by crushing of concrete, meaning the concrete reaches its allowable stress while the steel does not.

q: 19. The moment of resistance of an over-reinforced section is determined on the basis of ............
explain: In over-reinforced sections, the concrete is the limiting factor, so the moment of resistance is calculated based on the compressive capacity of the concrete.

q: 20. In a doubly reinforced beam, steel reinforcement is provided in a
explain: A doubly reinforced beam contains longitudinal reinforcement in both the tension and the compression zones to increase the moment capacity when dimensions are restricted.

q: 21. A doubly reinforced section in used
options: when the members are subjected to alternate external loads and the bending moment in the sections reverses
when the members are subjected to loading eccentric on either side of the axis
explain: Doubly reinforced sections are ideal for situations where moments reverse (like in seismic loading) or where the concrete alone cannot handle the compression due to eccentricity or restricted size.

q: 22. If the area of tensile steel reinforcement is doubled, the moment of resistance of the beam increases only by about
explain: Doubling the steel area shifts the neutral axis downward, reducing the lever arm and causing the concrete to reach its capacity faster. This leads to a non-proportional increase in moment capacity, roughly around 22%.

q: 23. In the steel beam theory of doubly reinforced concrete beams, it is assumed that
options: stress in compression steel is equal to stress in tension steel
in tension and compression concrete, no stress in developed
explain: Steel beam theory is a simplified method that assumes concrete provides no resistance at all, and the tension/compression are handled entirely by the steel at equal stress levels.

q: 24. The concrete below the neutral axis
explain: In reinforced concrete design, concrete in the tension zone (below the neutral axis) is assumed to be cracked and contributes nothing to bending resistance; its primary role is to provide cover and bond (embedment) for the steel.

q: 25. The breadth of rib in a T-beam should at least be equal to... the depth of rib.
explain: For structural stability and to avoid lateral buckling of the web, the breadth of the rib is generally recommended to be at least 1/3 of the depth of the rib.

q: 26. Thought the effective depth of a T-beam is the distance between the top compression edge to centre of the tensile reinforcement, for heavy loads, it is taken as
explain: For heavy loading conditions in flanged beams, a stiffer section is required, typically leading to an effective depth around 1/12 of the span.

q: 27. The partial factor of safety for concrete in limit state design is
explain: The partial safety factor for concrete (γc) is 1.50, reflecting higher uncertainty in site-mixed concrete compared to steel.

q: 28. A continuous beam shall be deemed to be a deep beam if the ratio of effective span to overall depth, is
explain: According to IS 456, a beam is considered deep when the L/D ratio is less than 2.0 for a simply supported beam and less than 2.5 for a continuous beam.

q: 29. A reinforced concrete beam subjected to a monotonously increasing load may fail at
explain: A beam design ensures that it only fails when it reaches its ultimate capacity (Ultimate Strength Stage).

q: 30. The ratio of the depth of the parabolic and rectangular portion block at the limit state of collapse of a singly reinforced section is
explain: In the IS 456 stress block, the rectangular portion is 3/7th and the parabolic portion is 4/7th of the neutral axis depth. The ratio 4/7 : 3/7 is 4:3.

q: 31. Tension failure occurs is singly reinforced beam in
explain: In an under-reinforced beam, the steel yields first. This provides ample warning (cracking and deflection) before the concrete eventually crushes, termed a tension failure.

q: 32. For the design purpose of flexural members, the partial safety factor for stress in the reinforcement
explain: The partial safety factor for steel (γs) is 1.15.

q: 33. A double reinforced beam may be provided from
explain: Doubly reinforced beams are used when depth is limited (headroom/architecture) or to increase ductility and resist reversal of moments (structural).

q: 34. The maximum diameter of the reinforcement bars in R.C.C. beams is limited to
options: one-eighth of the least dimension of the beams
one-tenth of the depth of beams
explain: General detailing guidelines suggest bar diameter should not exceed 1/8th of the least dimension to ensure bond and concrete flow.

q: 35. The minimum factor of safety against overturning for a retaining wall is
explain: Stability requirements dictate a minimum factor of safety of 2.0 against overturning to account for soil variations.

q: 36. Reinforcement is normally used in cast-in-situ concrete to
explain: Even if the member doesn't carry external tension, reinforcement is necessary to control cracking caused by temperature and shrinkage.

q: 37. The ultimate load used in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structures refers to
options: working loads multiplied by load factors
explain: Ultimate load = Characteristic Load × Load Factor.

q: 38. The ultimate strength of an under reinforced R.C.C. beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of the concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: The strength of an under-reinforced beam is limited by the amount of steel provided.

q: 39. The ultimate strength of an over reinforced R.C.C. beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of the concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In over-reinforced beams, concrete fails before the steel reaches its yield strength.

q: 40. The primary compression failure in R.C.C. beam is caused in
explain: Over-reinforced beams fail suddenly due to concrete crushing (primary compression failure).

q: 41. The ratio of the allowable ultimate crushing stress of beam in bending to that of 150 mm cube strength is
explain: Due to size effect and difference between lab and site, strength in the structure is taken as 0.67fck.

q: 42. The combined load factor applied in the ultimate strength design of R.C.C. structures is
explain: The most common partial safety factor for loads (Dead Load + Live Load) is 1.5.

q: 43. In prestressed concrete structures the prestressing of the concrete is done to compensate the stresses caused by
explain: Prestressing is designed to counteract the tensile stresses produced by the total working loads (the combination of dead and live loads) during the service life of the structure.

q: 44. The net effect due to prestressing in prestressed concrete beams is usually
explain: Prestressing introduces a longitudinal compressive force and a bending moment (due to eccentricity) which counteracts the downward bending from external loads.

q: 45. When the pile is suspended from two points, the minimum B.M. will occur if the overhang from each support is
explain: For a beam or pile suspended at two points, the maximum positive and negative bending moments are minimized when the overhang is approximately 0.207L (often rounded to 0.206L).

q: 46. The major loss of pre-stress is caused due to
explain: Loss of prestress occurs due to immediate factors (elastic shortening) and time-dependent factors (creep, shrinkage, and steel relaxation).

q: 47. The percentage minimum reinforcement of the gross sectional area in slabs, is
explain: IS 456 specifies 0.15% for mild steel bars and 0.12% for HYSD bars. 0.15% is the standard general minimum.

q: 48. The weight of reinforced concrete, is generally taken as
explain: Plain concrete is 2400 kg/m³, while reinforced concrete (RCC) is taken as 2500 kg/m³ to account for the higher density of steel.

q: 49. The ratio of the breadth to effective depth of a beam is kept
explain: For economical and structural efficiency, the breadth of a beam is typically half (0.50) of its effective depth.

q: 50. Design of R.C.C. simply supported beams carrying U.D.L. is based on the resultant B.M. at
explain: For a simply supported beam with UDL, the maximum bending moment (wl²/8) occurs at the mid-span, which governs the flexural design.

q: 51. Steel beam theory is used for
options: doubly reinforced beams ignoring compressive stress in concrete
beams if shear exceeds 4 times allowable shear stress
explain: Steel beam theory assumes that all compressive and tensile forces are carried by the steel reinforcement, ignoring the contribution of concrete in the compression zone.
